newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian GDP firms in first quarter, inflation low.
newsitem.headline: Australian GDP firms in first quarter, inflation low.

text.p: The Australian economy firmed in the quarter ended March 31, accelerating away from a flat spot in 1996 and showing little sign of inflationary pressure, official data released on Wednesday showed.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 0.9 percent from the previous quarter, accelerating from the previous quarterly growth rate of 0.4 percent, and stood 2.4 percent above its level a year earlier, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said.
Demand in the economy grew faster than production, and the gap was covered with a rundown in inventories of goods held by business, the figures showed.
Treasurer Peter Costello said the inventory rundown could not continue forever and GDP would have to accelerate further as 1997 wore on to meet demand.

"The composition of activity in the quarter, with very strong growth in final demand and a sharp rundown in non-farm stocks combined with other indicators of activity, suggest the economy is poised for an acceleration in growth," Costello said in a statement.

"The real story is in domestic demand, which troughed last September quarter and is now rising at its fastest quarterly rate for 2-1/2 years," said analyst Chris Richardson of economic forecasting firm Access Economics.
The GDP figures showed the economy in the sixth year of a prolonged expansion phase.
After a 1990/91 recession, the economy moved first sluggishly and then soared in late 1994. Growth generally declined after the 1994 boom and by late 1996 it had hit a flat spot.
The Reserve Bank of Australia, anticipating the slowdown, began cutting interest rates in July, 1996.
On May 23 it cited a continuing benign inflation outlook as it made its fourth successive 0.5 percentage point cut, taking overnight cash rates to 5.5 percent.

Wednesday's data backed that prognosis when the GDP deflator, a broad measure of inflation, rose just 0.3 percent in the March quarter, compared with 0.5 percent in the previous quarter. Its annual rate slipped to 1.6 percent.
"(It's) very much in line with numbers the Reserve Bank would be wanting to see, and it's certainly quite a good inflation indicator," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland told Reuters.

Market analysts are divided on the chances for a fifth interest rate cut. Some say the economy has a strong enough outlook to not need it; others argue that with inflation so low the central bank can afford to boost the economy again.

"There is no sign of price pressure," Colonial State Bank senior economist Craig James said. "The Australian economy can afford to grow more quickly and as such an easing of monetary policy is still likely."
The government forecasts that annual economic growth will average 3.75 percent in the fiscal year to June 1998.
The GDP data had little impact on financial markets.
Australia's foreign debt meanwhile continued its almost relentless rise in the March quarter to nudge A$200 billion (US$152 billion), official data also released on Wednesday showed.
The bureau said net foreign debt was A$199.90 billion at the end of March, up A$13.6 billion on a year before and representing 39.4 percent of GDP, compared with 38.7 percent in March 1996.
